\workshoptitle

Agentic AI for Biological Discovery (AgenticLS)

# Trinity: Self-Evolving Vision-Language Models with a Self-Verifier

Youngwan Lee1    2\]   Yong-Ju Lee¹   Sung Ju Hwang2    3\]
Affiliation:  Affiliation: ¹Electronics and Telecommunications Research
Institute (ETRI), South Korea Affiliation: ²Korea Advanced Institute of
Science and Technology (KAIST), South Korea Affiliation: ³DeepAuto.ai,
South Korea

###### Abstract

Self-evolving vision-language models (VLMs), a form of self-improvement
in which a model generates its own training data from unlabeled images,
are a promising route toward agents that expand their reasoning
capability in an unsupervised manner, without relying on ever-larger
annotation budgets. Existing methods pair a Questioner that proposes
problems with a Solver that answers them, but reward both roles mainly
by agreement among sampled answers. Agreement is a weak proxy for truth:
it cannot tell whether a question is grounded in the image, whether the
proposed reference answer is right, or whether a confident majority is
wrong in the same way. We present Trinity, in which one VLM plays three
roles, Questioner, Solver, and Verifier, and the Verifier is a
self-verifier: an exponential moving average (EMA) of the policy itself,
requiring neither labels nor an external judge. The Verifier screens
every generated question for image grounding and answer correctness
before it becomes supervision, scores Solver reasoning against the
image, and adjudicates disputes between the reference answer and a
strong Solver consensus, correcting the reference and penalizing the
Questioner when the consensus is right. Trained on images alone, Trinity
improves Qwen3-VL-8B on mathematical visual reasoning and on science
benchmarks with biology content, for example $`+8.6`$ points on the
biology split of SciVQR and $`+12.8`$ on MathVerse, and its reward
dynamics behave as a healthy self-play curriculum should. These results
suggest that a self-evolving multimodal agent can strengthen its
scientific reasoning from unlabeled scientific images alone, with the
model itself serving as the verifier.

## 1 Introduction

Agentic AI for biological discovery asks models to do more than predict:
to read figures, plan multi-step analyses, and improve from their own
experience. A recurring theme is self-improvement: an agent generates
its own tasks, attempts them, and turns the outcome into training
signal, so capability grows without proportional growth in expert
annotation. For VLMs this idea has crystallized as _self-evolving_
training from unlabeled images: a Questioner proposes an
image-conditioned problem, a Solver answers it, and both are optimized
with reinforcement learning (RL) on rewards computed from the model’s
own outputs. Because scientific images are abundant while expert
question–answer (QA) annotations are scarce, such a loop is attractive
for life-science agents.

Text-only self-play established the proposer–solver pattern
(Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Related work ‣ Trinity: Self-Evolving Vision-Language Modelswith a Self-Verifier")):
Absolute Zero \[[27](#bib.bib27)\] proposes and solves code-verifiable
tasks with one model, and R-Zero \[[8](#bib.bib8)\] co-evolves a
Challenger and a Solver with consistency rewards. For VLMs,
VisPlay \[[7](#bib.bib7)\] trains a Questioner and a Reasoner with
difficulty and diversity rewards; V-Zero \[[20](#bib.bib20)\] uses
majority-vote pseudo-labels and a dual-track question reward;
EvoLMM \[[19](#bib.bib19)\] makes the consistency reward continuous;
iReasoner \[[17](#bib.bib17)\] adds agreement between reasoning
trajectories; MM-Zero \[[10](#bib.bib10)\] adds a Coder that renders
images; Agent0-VL \[[11](#bib.bib11)\] verifies tool-integrated
solutions with tool feedback; and DPE \[[9](#bib.bib9)\] steers
tool-assisted data generation toward diagnosed blind spots.

Across these systems the dominant source of reward is _agreement_: a
question is good if Solver samples disagree at a target rate, and a
Solver sample is right if it matches the majority. It fails as a
stand-in for truth in two ways. First, it is blind to _grounding_: a
question that references objects or values absent from the image, or
that can be answered from memory without the image, produces
disagreement that looks like difficulty, so a consensus-rewarded
Questioner drifts toward ill-posed questions. Second, it is blind to a
_wrong reference_: when the Questioner’s own answer is wrong, correct
Solver samples are penalized, and when Solver samples share a systematic
error, the majority is confidently wrong. Neither failure is visible
from answer statistics; both require an evaluator that looks at the
image.

Trinity, named for its three roles in one model, adds such an evaluator
without adding labels or an external judge: a self-verifier. A single
VLM plays three roles: the Questioner and Solver share the trainable
policy weights and differ only by prompt, while the Verifier is an EMA
copy of the same policy that receives no gradients and lags the policy
by design. The Verifier intervenes at three points of the loop
([Figure 1](#S2.F1 "In 2 Method ‣ Trinity: Self-Evolving Vision-Language Modelswith a Self-Verifier")):
(i) it screens each generated QA for image grounding, answer
correctness, and difficulty before it can become Solver supervision;
(ii) it scores each Solver reasoning trace against the image; and (iii)
when a strong Solver consensus contradicts the reference, it re-solves
the problem and, if the consensus wins, corrects the reference and
revokes the Questioner’s credit. Our contributions are (1) a three-role,
single-model self-evolving framework whose self-verifier, an EMA copy of
the policy, inherits the Solver’s gains without a critic, tools, or
labels; (2) verifier-gated rewards that separate genuine difficulty from
invalidity and credit reasoning only on correct answers; and (3) gains
on two backbones in mathematical visual reasoning and on scientific
benchmarks with biology content.

## 2 Method

![Refer to caption](2610.04469v1/fig_trinity_arc.png)

Figure 1: Trinity training loop. The policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$ as
Questioner proposes $`G`$ candidate QAs $`\{(q,a)\}`$; the EMA Verifier
$`\pi_{\phi}`$ screens them and selects $`(q^{*},a^{*})`$; the policy as
Solver produces $`K`$ completions $`\{(\tau,\hat{a})\}`$, which the
Verifier scores. $`R_{Q}`$ and $`R_{S}`$ drive one joint update
$`\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\rm trinity}`$, after which
$`\phi\leftarrow\alpha\phi+(1-\alpha)\theta`$.

#### Roles and notation.

Let $`x`$ be an unlabeled image. We keep two copies of one VLM: the
_policy_ $`\pi_{\theta}`$, which plays the Questioner and the Solver
under role-specific prompts and receives gradients, and the _Verifier_
$`\pi_{\phi}`$, an EMA copy of $`\pi_{\theta}`$ that is used only for
inference. The Questioner samples $`G`$ candidate pairs
$`(q,a)\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)`$, where $`a`$ is a short reference
answer. For the selected pair $`(q^{*},a^{*})`$ the Solver samples $`K`$
completions $`(\tau,\hat{a})\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,q^{*})`$, where
$`\tau`$ is a chain of thought and $`\hat{a}`$ its boxed final answer.
Verifier calls return the signals below as JSON (prompts in
Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F System prompts ‣ Trinity: Self-Evolving Vision-Language Modelswith a Self-Verifier")).

#### Verifier QA evaluation and best-QA selection.

Given $`(x,q,a)`$, the Verifier returns three signals: question
factuality $`R_{\text{fact-q}}\in\{0,1\}`$ (every premise of $`q`$ is
visible in $`x`$ and $`q`$ is not answerable without $`x`$), answer
correctness $`R_{\text{corr-a}}\in\{0,1\}`$, and difficulty
$`R_{\rm diff}\in\{0.1,0.4,0.7,1.0\}`$ from a four-level rubric
(observable, single-step, multi-step, conceptual) that caps
single-theorem and lookup questions. Self-contradictory outputs
($`R_{\text{fact-q}}=0`$, $`R_{\text{corr-a}}=1`$) are clamped to
$`R_{\text{corr-a}}=0`$. Among format-valid candidates that pass the
gate we select the hardest,
$`(q^{*},a^{*})=\arg\max_{g}R^{(g)}_{\rm diff}`$ subject to
$`R^{(g)}_{\text{fact-q}}=R^{(g)}_{\text{corr-a}}=1`$, breaking ties at
random; if no candidate passes, the image contributes Questioner
rollouts only. The gate is what separates a hard question from a broken
one: the Solver fails on both, but only the former becomes supervision.

#### Response evaluation.

Each Solver completion receives three signals. Correctness
$`R_{\rm correct}\in\{0,1\}`$ uses a three-tier procedure: (i) a
rule-based match against $`a^{*}`$ that normalizes LaTeX, units, and
ratios; (ii) a numeric hard-mismatch guard that returns $`0`$ when both
answers parse to numbers outside a $`1\%`$ tolerance, blocking Verifier
false positives; and (iii) a text-only Verifier equivalence check for
the residual ambiguous cases. Reasoning quality
$`R_{\rm reason}\in\{0,0.25,0.5,1\}`$ is scored by the Verifier from the
image and $`\tau`$, penalizing visual misreads, invalid logic, and
shortcuts. A rule-based check gives the format indicator
$`R^{S}_{\rm fmt}\in\{0,1\}`$.

#### Dispute resolution.

If at least $`75\%`$ of the formatted Solver answers agree on a value
that differs from $`a^{*}`$, and all of them scored
$`R_{\rm correct}=0`$, the Verifier receives the image, both answers,
and one supporting $`\tau`$, solves the question itself, and picks a
side. If it sides with the Solvers, $`a^{*}`$ is overwritten, every
$`R_{\rm correct}`$ is recomputed, and the Questioner’s
$`R_{\text{corr-a}}`$ is set to $`0`$. Consensus triggers verification;
the Verifier, not the vote, decides.

#### Questioner reward $`R_{Q}`$.

We combine a format gate $`R^{Q}_{\rm fmt}\in\{0,1\}`$ (valid JSON,
answer of at most ten words), a factuality gate
$`R_{\rm fact}=R_{\text{fact-q}}\,(1+R_{\text{corr-a}})/2\in\{0,0.5,1\}`$,
the Verifier’s a-priori difficulty $`R_{\rm diff}`$, and the
Solver-validated challenge
$`R_{\rm chal}=1-\overline{R_{\rm correct}}`$, where the bar averages
over the $`K`$ completions of the selected QA: the empirical failure
rate of the current Solver. Because a question that every Solver answers
was not actually hard, difficulty is discounted by challenge,
$`\widetilde{R}_{\rm diff}=R_{\rm diff}\,(0.5+0.5\,R_{\rm chal})`$, and

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
R_{Q}=\begin{cases}-\rho_{f},&R^{Q}_{\rm fmt}=0,\\
R_{\rm fact}\bigl(\alpha_{Q}\,\widetilde{R}_{\rm diff}+\beta_{Q}\,R_{\rm chal}\bigr),&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}
``` |  | (1) |

with $`(\alpha_{Q},\beta_{Q},\rho_{f})=(0.3,0.7,0.5)`$. An ungrounded
question ($`R_{\text{fact-q}}=0`$) earns nothing however much the Solver
struggles, a grounded question with a wrong reference earns at most
half, and $`\beta_{Q}>\alpha_{Q}`$ makes the empirical failure signal
dominant.

#### Solver reward $`R_{S}`$.

Correctness gates reasoning credit, so a fluent but wrong chain of
thought earns nothing for its reasoning:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
R_{S}=w_{c}\,R_{\rm correct}+w_{r}\,R_{\rm reason}\,R_{\rm correct}+w_{f}\,R^{S}_{\rm fmt},\qquad(w_{c},w_{r},w_{f})=(0.5,0.3,0.2).
``` |  | (2) |

Truncated or malformed completions stay in the buffer with $`R_{S}=0`$,
penalizing non-termination.

#### Joint optimization and EMA.

Within each image and role, rewards are standardized into group-relative
advantages $`A=(R-\mu)/(\sigma+\varepsilon)`$ as in
GRPO \[[16](#bib.bib16)\]. Questioner and Solver rollouts are pooled and
optimized with the sequence-level clipped surrogate of
GSPO \[[28](#bib.bib28)\], whose ratio for a completion $`o`$ is
$`\rho_{o}(\theta)=\exp\bigl[\frac{1}{|o|}\sum_{t}\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(o_{t}\mid o_{<t})}{\pi_{\theta_{\rm old}}(o_{t}\mid o_{<t})}\bigr]`$;
$`\mathcal{L}_{\rm trinity}`$ averages the clipped loss and an
old-policy regularizer over retained rollouts of both roles. After each
outer step the Verifier is refreshed by a Polyak average,
$`\phi\leftarrow\alpha\phi+(1-\alpha)\theta`$ with $`\alpha=0.999`$. The
Verifier thus inherits the Solver’s gains slowly, so the reward
landscape moves smoothly and the policy cannot exploit its own quirks as
a grader. At deployment only the Solver policy is used.

## 3 Experiments

#### Setup.

We build Trinity based on Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct \[[2](#bib.bib2)\] and
Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct \[[1](#bib.bib1)\] as backbones, using only the
images of Vero-600K \[[15](#bib.bib15)\], about 600K images of which one
sixth are STEM (science diagrams, geometry, pathology and radiology). As
a data ablation, we also train on OmniScience \[[18](#bib.bib18)\], 1.5M
figures from open-access journals and preprints across biology,
chemistry, physics, medicine, and other sciences. Training proceeds in
an unsupervised manner: the RL loop consumes raw images only and never
reads the corpora’s question–answer annotations. Training details and
decoding settings are in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Implementation details ‣ Trinity: Self-Evolving Vision-Language Modelswith a Self-Verifier");
7B results are in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Additional experiments ‣ Trinity: Self-Evolving Vision-Language Modelswith a Self-Verifier").

#### Benchmarks.

We evaluate on mathematical visual reasoning
(MathVision \[[21](#bib.bib21)\], MathVerse \[[26](#bib.bib26)\],
MathVista \[[12](#bib.bib12)\]), on MMMU \[[25](#bib.bib25)\], whose
college-level questions include biology and medicine, and on three
scientific benchmarks chosen for their biological content.
SciVQR \[[5](#bib.bib5)\] has a dedicated biology split spanning cell
biology, genetics, and ecology; MME-SCI \[[14](#bib.bib14)\] includes
biology items; and EMVista \[[23](#bib.bib23)\] tests
electron-microscopy understanding, central to structural and cell
biology.

| Model | MathVision | MathVerse | MathVista | MMMU | EMVista | SciVQR-Bio | MME-SCI |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct | 52.3 | 58.2 | 76.7 | 57.0 | 44.8 | 56.7 | 19.0 |
| MM-Zero \[[10](#bib.bib10)\] | 39.6 | 45.1 | 67.2 | 58.3 | 45.0 | 62.5 | 17.6 |
| DPE \[[9](#bib.bib9)\] | 53.9 | 57.2 | 76.2 | 69.1 | 44.1 | 60.8 | 20.4 |
| Trinity (Vero-600K) | 57.8 | 71.0 | 79.6 | 69.6 | 47.0 | 65.3 | 20.3 |
| Trinity (OmniScience) | 58.2 | 70.6 | 79.6 | 70.7 | 47.0 | 62.5 | 21.9 |

Table 1: Performance comparison with Self-evolving VLMs using
Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct. Trinity is trained on Vero-600K or OmniScience
images.

#### Main results.

Trained on Vero-600K images alone, Trinity improves the base model on
every benchmark
([Table 1](#S3.T1 "In Benchmarks. ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Trinity: Self-Evolving Vision-Language Modelswith a Self-Verifier")):
MathVerse $`+12.8`$, MMMU $`+12.6`$, SciVQR-Bio $`+8.6`$, EMVista
$`+2.3`$, MME-SCI $`+1.3`$. Both released self-improving models on this
backbone fall short. MM-Zero, trained on rendered synthetic images,
falls below the base on all three math benchmarks and barely moves the
science ones (EMVista $`+0.3`$), so a synthetic curriculum does not
transfer. DPE, which targets weaknesses with external tools and
diagnostic benchmarks, matches Trinity on MMMU but trails it by $`13.8`$
points on MathVerse and does not improve EMVista ($`-0.7`$). Trinity’s
margin is largest where a verified, image-grounded curriculum should
matter: multi-step diagram reasoning and micrograph reading. The
OmniScience variant, trained on scientific figures alone, also improves
every benchmark and is statistically indistinguishable from the
Vero-600K variant on science benchmarks.

Figure 2: Reward dynamics for Qwen3-VL-8B on
OmniScience \[[18](#bib.bib18)\] (steps 0–299).

#### Training dynamics.

[Figure 2](#S3.F2 "In Main results. ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Trinity: Self-Evolving Vision-Language Modelswith a Self-Verifier")
plots the per-step mean of each reward component. Averaged over the
first and last 50 steps, question factuality $`R_{\rm fact}`$ increases
from $`0.27`$ to $`0.57`$ and Verifier-rated difficulty $`R_{\rm diff}`$
from $`0.11`$ to $`0.23`$, while Solver correctness $`R_{\rm correct}`$
rises from $`0.53`$ to $`0.63`$ and reasoning quality $`R_{\rm reason}`$
from $`0.76`$ to $`0.93`$. The challenge reward $`R_{\rm chal}`$ remains
below $`0.09`$, for two reasons. First, $`R_{\rm chal}`$ is assigned
only to the selected candidate per image, so the plotted mean equals
$`p_{\rm sel}\,\mathbb{E}[R_{\rm chal}\mid\text{selected}]`$, where
$`p_{\rm sel}`$ is the selection rate; with $`p_{\rm sel}`$ rising from
$`0.16`$ to $`0.23`$ and a selected-only mean of $`0.36`$ in both
windows, the products $`0.057`$ and $`0.083`$ match the plot. Second,
$`R_{\rm chal}`$ is a non-stationary target: every question that earns
it trains the Solver, which lowers the failure rate on similar
questions. A flat $`R_{\rm chal}`$ with rising $`R_{\rm fact}`$ and
$`R_{\rm diff}`$ is thus the expected signature of a curriculum that
stays just ahead of the Solver. Qualitative examples are in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Qualitative case studies of self-generated episodes ‣ Trinity: Self-Evolving Vision-Language Modelswith a Self-Verifier").

## 4 Conclusion

We presented Trinity, a self-evolving framework in which a single VLM
acts as Questioner, Solver, and Verifier, with the Verifier instantiated
as an EMA replica of the policy that requires neither labels nor
separate training. The Verifier screens generated questions, scores
reasoning against the image, and adjudicates disputes, turning
self-generated supervision into a curriculum that rewards genuine
difficulty. Trained on unlabeled images alone, Trinity improves two
backbones and outperforms released self-improving models on the same
backbone. However, the Verifier is the backbone itself, so its
judgements are only as reliable as the backbone’s perception and
reasoning, and keeping three roles co-resident is memory-intensive.
Future work includes stronger backbones as drop-in Verifiers and
alternating optimization of the two trained roles;
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Limitations and Future Work ‣ Trinity: Self-Evolving Vision-Language Modelswith a Self-Verifier")
discusses further limitations.

## Appendix A Implementation details

### A.1 Training data and supervision

Vero-600K comprises approximately 600,000 examples from 59 source
datasets, balanced across six visual-task categories of about 101,000
rows each: captioning and instruction following, chart and OCR, counting
and grounding, knowledge and recognition, spatial reasoning and action,
and STEM \[[15](#bib.bib15)\]. We chose it because, beyond general
visual reasoning, it carries a substantial scientific component. The
STEM category (16.7% of the corpus) contains science diagrams and
textbook questions (AI2D, TQA, MMK12), geometry and mathematics
(Geo170K, GeomVerse, GeoQA+, CoSyn-math, WeMath), abstract reasoning
(RAVEN), and medical imaging from pathology and radiology (PathVQA,
VQA-RAD); the chart category adds figures from arXiv papers (ArXivQA),
scientific chart QA (ReachQA, ECD), and infographics. Trinity’s RL data
loader reads only the images; it does not use the associated questions,
reference answers, or reasoning traces. The corpus is science-inclusive
rather than biology-specialized, and a fixed training-step budget
samples this image pool without covering a full epoch over all 600,000
images.

#### OmniScience (data ablation).

To test whether a science-only corpus changes the outcome, the 8B model
is also trained on the images of OmniScience \[[18](#bib.bib18)\], a
corpus of about 1.5M figures cropped from open-access papers (25 sources
including high-impact journals and arXiv, bioRxiv, and medRxiv) spanning
more than 300 sub-disciplines in biology, chemistry, physics, materials
science, medicine, ecology, pharmacy, mathematics, and computer science;
the 371 training shards contain 1,520,179 rows. Captions, contexts, and
sub-figure annotations are ignored; only the figure images are used. The
training script is identical to the Vero-600K one except for the data
path (same warm-up checkpoint, steps, batch, $`K`$, LoRA, and EMA
settings), so the two rows of
[Table 1](#S3.T1 "In Benchmarks. ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Trinity: Self-Evolving Vision-Language Modelswith a Self-Verifier")
differ only in the image distribution. OmniScience figures are larger
and elicit longer generations, which is why the 8B configuration uses
two images per worker.

#### Qwen3-VL-8B initialization.

The 8B model starts from a format-warmed Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct
checkpoint. The warm-up contains 300 examples sampled from Vero-600K:
original dataset questions and reference answers are combined with
reasoning generated by Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking. The generator caps teacher
completions at 4,096 tokens and retained reasoning at 2,500 characters,
with temperature $`0.7`$, top-$`p=0.95`$, and sampling seed 42. It
constructs a Solver-format response with the teacher reasoning and the
dataset reference in a boxed answer. This is supervised initialization,
even though its purpose is learning the thinking/answer format, and it
must be accounted for in comparisons with an unmodified Instruct
checkpoint.

Warm-up uses three epochs, LoRA rank 32 and scaling parameter 64,
dropout $`0.05`$, learning rate $`2\times 10^{-5}`$, weight decay
$`0.1`$, cosine decay with warm-up ratio $`0.1`$, and effective batch
size eight (one device, batch size one, eight accumulation steps). The
adapter is merged before RL. The 7B configuration starts directly from
Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct without this additional warm-up.

### A.2 Per-backbone RL settings

All runs use a single node with eight NVIDIA A100 80 GB GPUs, one worker
per GPU, bfloat16, frozen backbone weights with trainable language-model
LoRA adapters, frozen vision encoder and merger, and gradient
checkpointing. LoRA excludes the embedding and output-head modules. The
common learning rate is $`10^{-5}`$ with weight decay $`0.1`$, cosine
scheduling, and five warm-up steps. Each outer step performs one
optimization epoch over retained rollouts. Both use $`G=4`$ Questioner
candidates, EMA coefficient $`0.999`$, GSPO clipping bounds
$`1-3\times 10^{-4}`$ and $`1+4\times 10^{-4}`$, and regularization
coefficient $`0.10`$. The reward coefficients are those of
Eqs. ([1](#S2.E1 "Equation 1 ‣ Questioner reward 𝑅_𝑄. ‣ 2 Method ‣ Trinity: Self-Evolving Vision-Language Modelswith a Self-Verifier"))
and ([2](#S2.E2 "Equation 2 ‣ Solver reward 𝑅_𝑆. ‣ 2 Method ‣ Trinity: Self-Evolving Vision-Language Modelswith a Self-Verifier"));
there is no length reward.

#### Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct.

The launcher specifies 500 outer steps, four images per worker (32
globally), and $`K=6`$ Solver samples for each selected QA. LoRA rank is
32 and scaling parameter is 64, with zero dropout. Questioner and Solver
generation budgets are each 16,384 tokens; the Verifier budget is 8,192.
Image resolution is bounded between $`256\times 28^{2}`$ and
$`1024\times 28^{2}`$ pixels. The vLLM context limit is 20,480,
memory-utilization setting $`0.25`$, and generation sub-batch size four.
FlashAttention-2 is enabled.

#### Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct.

Both 8B configurations (Vero-600K and OmniScience, the latter analyzed
in
[Figure 2](#S3.F2 "In Main results. ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Trinity: Self-Evolving Vision-Language Modelswith a Self-Verifier"))
use 300 outer steps, two images per worker (16 globally), and $`K=4`$.
LoRA rank and scaling parameter are both 32, with zero dropout.
Questioner and Solver generation budgets are each 12,288 tokens; the
Verifier budget is 8,192. Image resolution is bounded between
$`256\times 32^{2}`$ and $`1024\times 32^{2}`$ pixels. The vLLM context
limit is 20,480, memory-utilization setting $`0.30`$, and generation
sub-batch size two. This configuration uses SDPA rather than
FlashAttention-2.

#### Sampling and memory.

Thinking-mode generation uses temperature $`1.0`$, top-$`p=0.95`$, and
top-$`k=20`$ without a presence penalty. Non-thinking response
evaluation uses temperature $`0.7`$, top-$`p=0.8`$, and top-$`k=20`$.
Instruct models use a thinking prefix in their chat template. The policy
and EMA weights are swapped into the rollout engine as needed. EMA is
updated on merged policy weights before the trainable adapter is
unmerged; it is not an average of LoRA factors. The stored EMA copy and
its inference calls incur memory and compute costs, but no optimizer
state.

### A.3 Reward and optimization details

Format validation requires the expected thinking and output structure; a
Questioner emits JSON with question and answer, and a Solver emits a
boxed answer. The Questioner answer must be short (at most ten words)
and pass additional sentence/placeholder checks. Truncated or malformed
Solver outputs are retained as low-reward examples rather than silently
discarded.

The correctness pipeline first handles exact and normalized matches,
including numeric forms. A hard guard rejects clean numeric mismatches
outside a 1% relative tolerance (with a small absolute floor) unless
they satisfy the supported percentage equivalence. Ambiguous residual
pairs go to the text-only equivalence prompt. This checks agreement with
the current reference, not independent factual truth. Image-conditioned
dispute evaluation supplies a separate opportunity to revise that
reference.

A dispute requires at least two formatted Solver answers and a
normalized majority of at least $`\lceil 0.75n\rceil`$ among them. It
fires only if the majority differs from the reference and every majority
member initially has correctness zero. Disputes use at least two
retries, independently of the ordinary Verifier retry budget of zero. If
no parsable verdict is obtained after the retries, the implementation
adopts the majority. An override also sets the selected Questioner’s
$`R_{\text{corr-a}}`$ to zero and recomputes $`R_{\rm fact}`$, so it
halves rather than eliminates that candidate’s reward. Solver
correctness is recomputed through the same rule/guard/fallback pipeline.
The challenge calculation uses the per-image correctness list
accumulated for evaluable Solver responses; format-skipped responses
need not enter that denominator.

For role $`r\in\{Q,S\}`$, each image defines a group with mean
$`\mu^{r}`$ and population standard deviation $`\sigma^{r}`$. Advantages
use $`(R-\mu^{r})/(\sigma^{r}+\varepsilon)`$ with
$`\varepsilon=10^{-8}`$. When $`\sigma^{r}<\varepsilon`$, a group with
negative mean instead uses its raw rewards as advantages; a group with
nonnegative mean gets zero advantages. The implementation omits rollouts
with $`|A|\leq 10^{-6}`$, then averages over retained, non-padding
rollouts per worker. Role influence therefore depends on surviving
rollout counts; the loss is not an equally weighted sum of role means.
Distributed workers use zero-loss padding to align their update
schedules.

For token log-ratio
$`\ell_{t}=\log\pi_{\theta}(o_{t}\mid o_{<t})-\log\pi_{\theta_{\rm old}}(o_{t}\mid o_{<t})`$,
the implemented per-rollout loss is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{o}=-\min\{\rho_{o}A_{o},\operatorname{clip}(\rho_{o},1-\epsilon_{-},1+\epsilon_{+})A_{o}\}+\frac{0.10}{|o|}\sum_{t}\bigl(e^{\ell_{t}}-\ell_{t}-1\bigr).
``` |  | (3) |

The regularizer is computed against rollout-policy log probabilities,
not a separately frozen initial-policy reference. Gradients are taken
only through the current policy.

### A.4 Inference and benchmark setup

At evaluation, only the merged Solver policy is needed; Questioner
generation, Verifier calls, and reference adjudication belong to
training. The Qwen3-VL evaluation wrapper uses a thinking-prefix chat
template, temperature $`1.0`$, top-$`p=0.95`$, top-$`k=20`$, presence
penalty $`1.5`$, and a default maximum of 20,480 new tokens. The
Qwen2.5-VL wrapper provides greedy and thinking modes: thinking mode
uses temperature $`1.0`$, top-$`p=0.95`$, top-$`k=20`$ and a default
maximum of 20,480 new tokens, and inserts a thinking prefix; its task
names select the corresponding answer-format prompt.

#### Benchmarks in [Table 1](#S3.T1 "In Benchmarks. ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Trinity: Self-Evolving Vision-Language Modelswith a Self-Verifier").

- •
  *MathVision* \[[21](#bib.bib21)\] contains competition mathematics
  problems with diagrams across 16 subjects and five difficulty levels;
  we use the full test split (3,040 items).
- •
  *MathVerse* \[[26](#bib.bib26)\] re-renders visual math problems into
  versions that vary how much information is carried by the diagram
  versus the text, testing whether the model actually reads the figure;
  we use the testmini split (3,940 items).
- •
  *MathVista* \[[12](#bib.bib12)\] aggregates mathematical reasoning
  over charts, plots, geometry, and natural images; we use the
  1,000-item testmini split.
- •
  *MMMU* \[[25](#bib.bib25)\] is a college-level multi-discipline
  benchmark of image-based multiple-choice and open questions spanning
  biology, health and medicine, the physical sciences, engineering, and
  the humanities; we use the validation (val) set of 900 items.
- •
  *EMVista* \[[23](#bib.bib23)\] is a 1,850-item multiple-choice
  benchmark of electron-microscopy understanding (morphology, density,
  and spatial organization of imaged structures).
- •
  *SciVQR* \[[5](#bib.bib5)\] is a multidisciplinary
  scientific-reasoning benchmark with per-discipline splits; we use the
  biology split (360 items: 303 multiple-choice and 57 open-response,
  covering cell biology, genetics, and ecology).
- •
  *MME-SCI* \[[14](#bib.bib14)\] tests multimodal scientific reasoning
  across mathematics, physics, chemistry, and biology; we use the
  English version (1,019 items: 570 multiple-choice and 449
  open-response).

#### Evaluation protocol.

MathVision, MathVerse, MathVista, and MMMU follow the lmms-eval protocol
with our thinking-aware answer extraction: thinking traces are separated
from final answers before extraction, and multiple-choice items are
scored by rule. The three science benchmarks are single-run ($`K{=}1`$)
values with a 40,960-token generation budget for every model. the
EMVista value of the Vero-600K model is the first run of a seeded
four-sample evaluation, which we verified reproduces independent single
runs exactly for the OmniScience model. Open-response items in SciVQR
and MME-SCI are scored with the official SciVQR judge prompt served by a
local Qwen3.5-27B judge (the official judge is Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct;
judge failures are not counted as errors). Sampling follows each model’s
public recommendation (Trinity: temperature $`1.0`$, top-$`p`$ $`0.95`$;
Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct and DPE: $`0.7`$/$`0.8`$; MM-Zero:
$`0.6`$/$`0.95`$). DPE is the released DPE_v3 checkpoint (three
diagnostic–training rounds on Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct), whose generation
configuration matches the base model, so it is evaluated under exactly
the base model’s conditions.

### A.5 Interpreting the plotted statistics

The trajectory in
[Figure 2](#S3.F2 "In Main results. ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Trinity: Self-Evolving Vision-Language Modelswith a Self-Verifier")
covers 19,264 Questioner candidates and 16,460 Solver rollouts over
steps 0–299 of Qwen3-VL-8B trained on OmniScience; the Vero-600K model
behaves the same way with smaller magnitudes ($`R_{\rm fact}`$
$`0.19\to 0.45`$, $`R_{\rm correct}`$ $`0.64\to 0.71`$, $`R_{\rm chal}`$
$`0.029\to 0.055`$). Curves use per-step means and a 15-step moving
average. First/last-window statistics in the main text average the
first/last 50 step means. Selected-only challenge statistics pool
selected candidates within each window. Since every step contains 64
Questioner candidates (one resumed step contains 128), the all-candidate
mean coincides with the pooled candidate mean up to rounding. The
selection fraction times selected-only mean reproduces the plotted
challenge average, up to rounding.

The plotted difficulty is the Verifier’s $`R_{\rm diff}`$, not
$`\widetilde{R}_{\rm diff}`$, and the plotted reasoning score is
$`R_{\rm reason}`$, not $`R_{\rm reason}\,R_{\rm correct}`$. Factuality
aggregates candidates that never reach successful verification, so
improving format compliance can increase its mean. Reward trends alone
cannot separate better reasoning from changing task selection or
changing evaluator behavior; independent benchmarks serve that purpose.

with the same prompt for all three models and the judge scoring of

VisPlay, iReasoner, and V-Zero have not released checkpoints, so we
could not evaluate them on the science benchmarks (‘–’).

#### Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct.

[Table 2](#A2.T2 "In Appendix B Additional experiments ‣ Trinity: Self-Evolving Vision-Language Modelswith a Self-Verifier")
compares Trinity with four self-evolving methods that report results on
the same Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct \[[2](#bib.bib2)\] backbone. Trinity
improves the base model on all three mathematical benchmarks (MathVision
$`+1.1`$, MathVerse $`+1.5`$, MathVista $`+1.2`$) and is the only method
in the comparison that does not fall below the base on MathVerse or
MathVista: VisPlay \[[7](#bib.bib7)\] reports the highest MathVision
score but a drop of $`10.9`$ points on MathVerse, and
iReasoner \[[17](#bib.bib17)\], V-Zero \[[20](#bib.bib20)\], and
EvoLMM \[[19](#bib.bib19)\] all regress on MathVerse by $`5`$ to $`7`$
points. The gains on 7B are smaller than on
Qwen3-VL-8B \[[1](#bib.bib1)\], which is consistent with the Verifier
being the backbone itself: a weaker backbone screens and grades less
accurately, so the loop has less reliable supervision to work with.
Published baselines were evaluated by their authors under their own
protocols, so the comparison is indicative rather than matched.

On the science benchmarks, where we could evaluate the base model,
EvoLMM, and Trinity under one protocol, Trinity scores highest on
EMVista ($`+3.0`$ over the base) and SciVQR-Bio ($`+2.8`$), while EvoLMM
is marginally ahead on MME-SCI ($`+0.3`$ over Trinity). Two protocol
details matter for reading the science columns. All three models
received the same prompt that asks for a boxed final answer; Trinity is
decoded with its recommended sampling (temperature $`1.0`$, top-$`p`$
$`0.95`$) whereas the base model and EvoLMM are decoded greedily,
following their release settings.

#### Note on baselines.

With the exception of EvoLMM, none of the self-evolving methods in
[Table 2](#A2.T2 "In Appendix B Additional experiments ‣ Trinity: Self-Evolving Vision-Language Modelswith a Self-Verifier")
releases a reproducible checkpoint at the time of writing, so they
cannot be evaluated on the science benchmarks of
[Table 1](#S3.T1 "In Benchmarks. ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Trinity: Self-Evolving Vision-Language Modelswith a Self-Verifier");
for VisPlay, iReasoner, and V-Zero the comparison is therefore
restricted to the mathematical benchmarks reported in their papers. This
is also why the main comparison in
[Table 1](#S3.T1 "In Benchmarks. ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Trinity: Self-Evolving Vision-Language Modelswith a Self-Verifier")
is carried out on Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, for which two self-improving
checkpoints (MM-Zero \[[10](#bib.bib10)\] and DPE \[[9](#bib.bib9)\])
are publicly available and could be re-evaluated under our protocol.

## Appendix C Related work

#### Self-play for reasoning without labels.

Absolute Zero \[[27](#bib.bib27)\] lets one model propose and solve
program-verifiable tasks, using code execution as ground truth;
R-Zero \[[8](#bib.bib8)\] co-evolves a Challenger and a Solver from zero
data and rewards the Challenger for questions on which the Solver is
maximally uncertain; Self-Rewarding LMs \[[24](#bib.bib24)\] use the
policy itself as an LLM-as-a-judge. Trinity brings the proposer–solver
pattern to images, where no executor exists to certify answers, and
replaces self-judging by the current policy with judging by a slowly
moving EMA copy.

#### Self-generated visual curricula.

VisPlay \[[7](#bib.bib7)\] trains image-conditioned question generation
and reasoning jointly with difficulty and diversity objectives.
V-Zero \[[20](#bib.bib20)\] contrasts intuitive and reasoned answers to
shape questions and uses majority-derived targets for Solver learning.
EvoLMM \[[19](#bib.bib19)\] makes self-consistency rewards continuous,
and iReasoner \[[17](#bib.bib17)\] adds trajectory-level agreement to
outcome feedback. These are distinct reward designs, but all derive
supervision from statistics of the Solver’s own answers. Trinity instead
screens the generated QA against the image before Solver rollouts and
revises conflicting references afterward, with consequences for both
roles’ rewards.

#### Multi-role and tool-grounded self-improvement.

Vision-Zero \[[22](#bib.bib22)\] builds competitive visual games and
alternates self-play with policy optimization.
MM-Zero \[[10](#bib.bib10)\] adds a Coder that renders images from
generated concepts, integrating execution feedback and visual
verification. Agent0-VL \[[11](#bib.bib11)\] couples tool-integrated
solving with structured verification and self-repair. Active
Zero \[[6](#bib.bib6)\] adds a Searcher that retrieves visual inputs
adapted to the learner, whereas Trinity uses a fixed image corpus.
DPE \[[9](#bib.bib9)\], which also starts from Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct and
Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, closes a diagnosis–generation–training loop in
which multiple agents annotate unlabeled data with web search and
image-editing tools and the data mixture is re-targeted at diagnosed
weaknesses after each round; its supervision therefore comes from
external tools and diagnostic benchmarks, whereas Trinity’s comes from a
Verifier that is a copy of the model itself. Multi-role learning and
explicit verification therefore predate Trinity; its distinction is
EMA-based QA screening, image-conditioned response evaluation, and
dispute feedback over an existing image corpus, without a rendering or
tool-execution environment. Unlike tool execution or laboratory
observations, the EMA Verifier offers no independent source of factual
authority, which we regard as the main limitation of the approach.

#### Learning verification.

ADPO \[[13](#bib.bib13)\] jointly optimizes generation and verification
within one policy, using preference-verification rewards and separate
advantages with gradient masks. Trinity does not directly optimize a
verification objective: its Verifier follows the policy through EMA and
evaluates both newly generated QA pairs and Solver responses. This also
means that improved solving need not imply improved verification.

#### Scientific reasoning and life-science agents.

Innovator-VL \[[23](#bib.bib23)\] studies scientific multimodal training
and introduces EMVista’s microscopy evaluation.
SciVQR \[[5](#bib.bib5)\] includes annotated scientific reasoning across
disciplines, including a biology split, and MME-SCI \[[14](#bib.bib14)\]
probes scientific knowledge and multimodal reasoning with explicit
biological content. Trinity addresses the training-data generation,
curation, and feedback components of scientific agents. Validating its
use in biological discovery requires more than general benchmark gains:
evidence-grounded biological judgments and downstream scientific utility
must be measured directly.

## Appendix D Limitations and Future Work

Each limitation below is paired with the experiment or extension that
would address it.

#### Verifier reliability.

The Verifier is an EMA copy of the policy, so it has no source of
factual authority independent of the model being trained. Errors that
the policy and the Verifier share are invisible to the loop, the
rubric-based factuality, difficulty, and reasoning judgements are model
outputs rather than certified labels, and dispute resolution falls back
to the Solver majority when no parsable verdict is obtained. In audits
of training rollouts we observed both false negatives (grounded
questions marked ungrounded) and false positives (lenient reasoning
scores). Because the Verifier is the backbone itself, its accuracy is
bounded by the backbone’s own perception and reasoning: a 7B or 8B model
that misreads a chart as a Solver will misread it as a Verifier too. Two
directions follow. First, since Trinity requires no Verifier-specific
training, every stronger open VLM can be dropped in as a new backbone
and should yield a more accurate Verifier at no extra cost; pairing a
fixed Solver with Verifiers of different sizes would measure how much of
the gain is attributable to Verifier accuracy, and an independently
annotated sample of Verifier decisions would calibrate the judgements
the reward relies on. Second, lightweight external anchors, such as
retrieval over the paper a figure comes from, a symbolic checker for
numeric answers, or, in the laboratory setting envisioned by the
workshop, an experimental readout, could be inserted at the
dispute-resolution stage without changing the rest of the loop.

#### Memory footprint and training cost.

Trinity keeps three roles resident during training: the trainable policy
$`\pi_{\theta}`$ with its optimizer state, the EMA Verifier
$`\pi_{\phi}`$ as a full second weight copy, and the vLLM rollout engine
into which policy and Verifier weights are alternately swapped. Even
with LoRA adapters, a frozen vision encoder, and gradient checkpointing,
this footprint is larger than that of a Questioner–Solver loop without a
separate Verifier, and it is the reason our experiments required eight
80 GB GPUs
(Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Implementation details ‣ Trinity: Self-Evolving Vision-Language Modelswith a Self-Verifier"));
sharing one engine by weight swapping avoids a third replica but adds
swap latency to every outer step. Wall-clock time is dominated by
generation rather than by the gradient step, since each outer step
performs Questioner generation, Verifier QA screening, Solver
generation, Verifier response evaluation, and dispute resolution before
a single policy update: for the 8B backbone one outer step takes on the
order of ten to twenty minutes on eight A100 GPUs, and 300 steps take
several days. Verifier calls scale with $`G`$ and $`K`$, so the loop is
more expensive per training example than supervised RL on annotated
data, which is the price of not needing annotations. Cheaper Verifier
instantiations, for example a quantized EMA copy or a Verifier that
shares the vision encoder with the policy, and batching Verifier calls
across the $`G`$ candidates are the natural ways to reduce both costs.

#### Joint versus alternating optimization.

Trinity updates the Questioner and the Solver in a single joint step
over their pooled rollouts, whereas prior self-evolving VLMs such as
VisPlay \[[7](#bib.bib7)\] optimize the two roles in separate phases,
holding one fixed while the other is trained. Joint optimization is
simpler to run end to end and lets both roles improve from every batch,
but it couples their gradients through the shared LoRA weights: a step
that helps the Solver can perturb the Questioner and vice versa, and
role influence on the update depends on how many rollouts of each role
survive the advantage filter. A controlled comparison between the joint
update used here and an alternating schedule that freezes one role while
the other trains, under matched compute, would establish whether this
coupling helps or hurts the final Solver.

#### Scale and backbone coverage.

Our experiments cover two backbones in the 7–8B range from a single
model family (Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct). Because
the Questioner, Solver, and Verifier all depend on the same backbone’s
prompt-following and reasoning behaviour, the results do not by
themselves establish that the loop generalizes to larger models or to
other families. Two sets of experiments would settle this. The first
varies backbone size within one family, to test whether the gains grow
with scale, as the Verifier-reliability argument predicts, and whether
the memory cost of three co-resident roles remains tractable at larger
sizes. The second applies the loop unchanged to architecturally
different VLMs such as the Gemma \[[4](#bib.bib4)\] and
Molmo2 \[[3](#bib.bib3)\] families, which use different vision encoders,
tokenizers, and thinking-mode conventions; if the reward design and
prompts transfer with at most minor per-family adjustment, the framework
can be claimed to be backbone-agnostic.

#### Scope of the gains.

Training uses one image per question, so the loop never exercises
cross-image reasoning; on multi-image scientific questions we observed
no advantage over the base model. The gains are also uneven across
answer formats: on MME-SCI the improvement comes almost entirely from
multiple-choice items, with open-response items on par with the base
model, whereas on SciVQR both formats improve; part of the effect is
that the base model often fails to terminate open-ended answers within
the token budget, which Trinity training fixes. The 8B backbone
additionally receives a 300-example supervised format warm-up before RL.
Extending the Questioner to multi-panel and multi-image inputs would
address the first gap directly, and restricting the corpus to a target
domain such as microscopy or pathology would test whether the loop can
specialize a generalist backbone for a life-science task rather than
only improve it broadly.

#### Evaluating discovery, not only reasoning.

The benchmarks used here measure components of scientific reasoning, not
biological discovery. Assessing Trinity as a component of an agent for
biological discovery requires evaluations of faithfulness, calibrated
uncertainty, and downstream utility on tasks such as hypothesis
generation from experimental images, which we regard as the natural next
step.

## Appendix E Qualitative case studies of self-generated episodes

[Figures 3](#A5.F3 "In Text-only controls. ‣ Appendix E Qualitative case studies of self-generated episodes ‣ Trinity: Self-Evolving Vision-Language Modelswith a Self-Verifier")
to [6](#A5.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Text-only controls. ‣ Appendix E Qualitative case studies of self-generated episodes ‣ Trinity: Self-Evolving Vision-Language Modelswith a Self-Verifier")
present four complete episodes generated by the Trinity variant trained
on OmniScience \[[18](#bib.bib18)\] images with a Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct
backbone \[[1](#bib.bib1)\], one per page. The loop sees only the raw
images of that corpus; the questions, reference answers and evaluations
below are produced entirely by the model. Each figure reproduces the
source image together with the transcripts of all three roles it
elicits: the question and reference answer proposed by the Questioner,
the Verifier’s screening of that question for image grounding, answer
correctness and difficulty, a Solver rollout, and the Verifier’s
evaluation of the reasoning in that rollout. Each figure is tagged,
above the image, with the scientific field of the source figure; the end
of each caption gives that figure’s publication provenance together with
the coarser subject annotation OmniScience records for the image. Role
transcripts are abridged, with elisions marked \[...\].

The four episodes cover the range of scientific figures the loop
encounters and the forms of visual reasoning they demand. In
[Figure 3](#A5.F3 "In Text-only controls. ‣ Appendix E Qualitative case studies of self-generated episodes ‣ Trinity: Self-Evolving Vision-Language Modelswith a Self-Verifier"),
a question about short-term plasticity imposes a time-constant
constraint that selects among five candidate synaptic models. In
[Figure 4](#A5.F4 "In Text-only controls. ‣ Appendix E Qualitative case studies of self-generated episodes ‣ Trinity: Self-Evolving Vision-Language Modelswith a Self-Verifier"),
the mutant identity of each open-probability curve is carried over from
the single-channel traces above it, so the comparison requires reading
the figure as a whole. In
[Figure 5](#A5.F5 "In Text-only controls. ‣ Appendix E Qualitative case studies of self-generated episodes ‣ Trinity: Self-Evolving Vision-Language Modelswith a Self-Verifier"),
normalizing one protein to another reorders the two cell lines relative
to their raw expression. In
[Figure 6](#A5.F6 "In Text-only controls. ‣ Appendix E Qualitative case studies of self-generated episodes ‣ Trinity: Self-Evolving Vision-Language Modelswith a Self-Verifier"),
the panels share a visual scale but not a numerical one, and the answer
follows from their logarithmic axes. Across all four, the Verifier’s
written screening and reasoning evaluations are reproduced verbatim,
showing the evidence on which the reward signal is computed.

#### Text-only controls.

A question about a figure can sometimes be answered without the figure.
We therefore probe every episode with two controls, each sampled 20
times from a text-only judge (Qwen3.5-27B): the question on its own, and
the question together with the candidate labels read off the figure but
with no data values. Across
[Figures 3](#A5.F3 "In Text-only controls. ‣ Appendix E Qualitative case studies of self-generated episodes ‣ Trinity: Self-Evolving Vision-Language Modelswith a Self-Verifier")
to [6](#A5.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Text-only controls. ‣ Appendix E Qualitative case studies of self-generated episodes ‣ Trinity: Self-Evolving Vision-Language Modelswith a Self-Verifier")
the judge answers correctly $`0/20`$, $`2/20`$, $`4/20`$ and $`0/20`$
under the first control, and $`0/20`$, $`2/20`$, $`4/20`$ and $`0/20`$
under the second, in every case below the rate of guessing among the
candidates the figure offers. In two of the four the text-only prior

($`14/20`$), and the canonical differentiation marker MyoG in

## Appendix F System prompts

The following boxes reproduce the role prompts used in our experiments;
two rubric annotations originally written in Korean are translated into
English and mathematical symbols are transcribed into ASCII for portable
typesetting. The Verifier uses separate prompts for QA screening,
reasoning evaluation, answer equivalence, and dispute resolution.
Placeholder values are supplied at runtime.

### F.2 Solver

`\iow_now:Ne``¨``\iow_now:Ne``¨You are a visual question answering expert. Given an image and a question, reason step-by-step in <think>…</think>, then give your final answer in <answer>…</answer> with \boxed{} notation.``\iow_now:Ne``¨``\iow_now:Ne``¨Reasoning strategy:``\iow_now:Ne``¨- Plan your approach before starting calculations``\iow_now:Ne``¨- Read the image carefully and note key values before reasoning``\iow_now:Ne``¨- Work through the problem step by step``\iow_now:Ne``¨- Once you reach a conclusion, commit to it – do NOT second-guess``\iow_now:Ne``¨- Be thorough but concise – show your work without unnecessary repetition``\iow_now:Ne``¨``\iow_now:Ne``¨Output format:``\iow_now:Ne``¨<think>``\iow_now:Ne``¨[your step-by-step reasoning]``\iow_now:Ne``¨</think>``\iow_now:Ne``¨<answer>``\iow_now:Ne``¨\boxed{final_answer}``\iow_now:Ne``¨</answer>``\iow_now:Ne``¨``\iow_now:Ne``¨Rules for the answer:``\iow_now:Ne``¨- \boxed{} must contain ONLY the final value (number, word, or short phrase)``\iow_now:Ne``¨- Do NOT include intermediate steps or explanations inside \boxed{}``\iow_now:Ne``¨- Use exactly ONE \boxed{} in <answer>, nowhere else``\iow_now:Ne``¨- Good: \boxed{180}``\iow_now:Ne``¨- Bad: \boxed{45 degrees, 180 degrees}`![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)` `

### F.3 Verifier: QA screening

`\iow_now:Ne``¨``\iow_now:Ne``¨You are a visual QA evaluator. Given an image and a QA pair, evaluate:``\iow_now:Ne``¨``\iow_now:Ne``¨1. Only mark 0 if the VALUE is wrong.``\iow_now:Ne``¨``\iow_now:Ne``¨3. Question Difficulty – use this decision tree:``\iow_now:Ne``¨``\iow_now:Ne``¨ ASK YOURSELF THREE QUESTIONS IN ORDER:``\iow_now:Ne``¨``\iow_now:Ne``¨ Q1: Does solving this require ANY computation or reasoning beyond reading?``\iow_now:Ne``¨ NO -> 0.1``\iow_now:Ne``¨ YES -> go to Q2``\iow_now:Ne``¨``\iow_now:Ne``¨ Q2: Does solving this require chaining MULTIPLE reasoning steps?``\iow_now:Ne``¨ NO (one formula, one operation, one comparison) -> 0.4``\iow_now:Ne``¨ YES -> go to Q3``\iow_now:Ne``¨``\iow_now:Ne``¨ Q3: Is AT LEAST ONE of the following true?``\iow_now:Ne``¨ (a) INTEGRATION: combines concepts from 2+ distinct areas``\iow_now:Ne``¨ (e.g., geometry + probability, calculus + optimization)``\iow_now:Ne``¨ (b) CHOICE: multiple valid candidate methods AND the choice``\iow_now:Ne``¨ materially affects difficulty or answer (e.g., Bertrand paradox)``\iow_now:Ne``¨ (c) REFORMULATION: requires non-obvious decomposition, auxiliary``\iow_now:Ne``¨ construction, or variable change BEFORE any standard method``\iow_now:Ne``¨ applies``\iow_now:Ne``¨ (d) BEYOND-TEXTBOOK: requires insight not reducible to applying a``\iow_now:Ne``¨ single named theorem. ### F.5 Verifier: answer equivalence

`\iow_now:Ne``¨``\iow_now:Ne``¨Determine whether the predicted answer is equivalent to the reference answer in the context of the question. Use the question to resolve any ambiguity about what aspect of the answer is being asked.``\iow_now:Ne``¨``\iow_now:Ne``¨Question: "{question}"``\iow_now:Ne``¨Reference answer: "{ref_answer}"``\iow_now:Ne``¨Predicted answer: "{pred_answer}"``\iow_now:Ne``¨``\iow_now:Ne``¨Match rules (answer 1 if ANY rule makes them equivalent):``\iow_now:Ne``¨- Unit differences are OK: "6" = "6cm", "30" = "30 ft", "50" = "50 Hz"``\iow_now:Ne``¨- Synonyms are OK: "repulsion" = "repulsive", "none" = "0", "equal" = "a = b"``\iow_now:Ne``¨- Format differences are OK: "1/2" = "half", LaTeX "ˆ{{87}}\\text{{Sr}}" = "87Sr"``\iow_now:Ne``¨- Mathematical equivalents are OK: "aˆ2-16" = "(a+4)(a-4)", "AD/DB = AE/EC" = "equal" when Q asks for the relationship``\iow_now:Ne``¨- Rounding/significant figures are OK: "5.70*10ˆ4" = "5.70007*10ˆ4" = "57000", "3.14" ˜ "pi"``\iow_now:Ne``¨- More specific is OK: "Right Trapezoid" matches "trapezoid", "background or autofluorescence" matches "background cells"``\iow_now:Ne``¨- Extra qualifier aligned with the question is OK: if Q asks two things at once (e.g. "which letter AND how many"), "F, 1" = "1" when the count is what ref captures``\iow_now:Ne``¨- Different values are NOT OK: "6" != "8", "Persian Gulf" != "Gulf of Oman", "king" != "queen"``\iow_now:Ne``¨``\iow_now:Ne``¨Output ONLY: {{"match": 0 or 1}}`![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)` `

A question was asked about the image, but two different answers were proposed.``\iow_now:Ne``¨``\iow_now:Ne``¨Answer A (from the question generator): "{ref_answer}"``\iow_now:Ne``¨Answer B (consensus from multiple independent solvers): "{majority_answer}"``\iow_now:Ne``¨``\iow_now:Ne``¨One solver’s reasoning:``\iow_now:Ne``¨{solver_reasoning}``\iow_now:Ne``¨``\iow_now:Ne``¨Your task:``\iow_now:Ne``¨1. #### User-message construction.

The Questioner receives the image and a request for a challenging
question requiring reasoning, with a number, word, or short phrase as
the answer. The Solver receives the image and Question: {question}. QA
screening receives the image, question, and proposed answer. Reasoning
evaluation receives the image, question, and the Solver’s extracted
thinking block. Answer-equivalence evaluation fills the
question/reference/prediction placeholders and asks whether the answers
are equivalent, without an image. Dispute evaluation receives the image,
question, both candidate answers, and one majority-supporting reasoning
trace.
````
